name: a-camcorder-sprinkler-garden
prompt: A single paused frame from a worn home-video tape recorded on a family camcorder in about 1998, cropped tall: a narrow back garden behind a red-brick British terraced house on a hot afternoon, patchy yellowing lawn, a wooden fence with a neighbour's washing line beyond it, and a cheap plastic oscillating sprinkler throwing a glittering fan of water across the grass. Two children, a girl of about seven in a faded pink swimsuit and a younger boy in baggy blue swim shorts, are caught mid-leap through the spray with arms flung out, mouths open in shrieking laughter, wet hair stuck to their foreheads. A child's bike lies on its side on the lawn by a paddling pool, and at the near edge of frame a parent's bare forearm and hand reach in, slightly blurred, as if pointing them out. The camera is held at an adult's waist height, wobbling and tilted a few degrees off level, the focus hunting so everything is gently soft. The look is analogue consumer video: low resolution, smeared fine detail, a faint horizontal smudge where the reds and pinks bleed past their edges, lifted milky blacks, blown-out white sky, slightly muted greens and warm yellow cast, a soft halo of glare around the water droplets, fine tape noise. Ordinary, unposed, a little clumsy, plainly joyful. No text, numbers, date stamp or on-screen markings anywhere in the image. Thanks.

name: a-flash-digicam-birthday
prompt: Vertical family snapshot from about 2002, shot on a cheap silver compact digital camera with a low-resolution CCD sensor, its tiny pop-up flash firing straight at the table: a crowded terraced-house lounge at night during a kid's sixth birthday. Framed tight and lopsided, horizon leaning to the right, the birthday girl sits low in the frame with a gappy grin and a crooked paper crown, lips pursed at five wobbling candles on a supermarket sponge cake smeared with blue icing. Behind her a scrum of cousins, a dad in a football shirt and a nan in a cardigan whoop with arms in the air; one lad sticks his tongue out, one aunt stares back with glowing red pupils. The flash flattens every face into bright shiny skin and blown-out white napkins, casts a hard black halo-shadow on the woodchip wallpaper, then dies within a couple of metres so the back of the room drops into a murky tangerine haze from a single standard lamp. Clutter crammed into the corners: helium balloons drifting against the artex ceiling, a party-ring biscuit plate, paper cups of fizzy pop, ripped gift wrap over a loud paisley carpet. Colour cranked and garish, warm-yellow cast, greenish noise blotches in the shadows, crunchy compression smearing the dark edges, a little soft from a plastic lens. Chaotic, loud, joyful. Leave the frame free of writing, date stamps, numbers or logos. Thanks.

name: a-disposable-film-seaside
prompt: A snapshot from a 1998 family day trip to the English coast, the sort of print that sat in a shoebox for twenty years and was scanned slightly skewed: shot with a single-use plastic film camera, fixed focus, one click of the winding wheel per frame. A gusty bright noon on a steep bank of grey pebbles. Front and centre a beaming grandad, shirt untucked, trouser legs turned up to the shins, pale bony ankles in the stones, punches a ninety-nine-style whippy cone up at the sky as if he has just won the cup final, white cream sliding down over his knuckles. Two little ones at his knees, a girl in a pink anorak with her hood whipped back and a boy in a football shirt, swing sand-pails and squint, one doubled over laughing; a nan perched on a stripy deckchair behind them, hand clamped on her hat. Behind the family a ragged line of candy-striped canvas breaks in faded red, blue and yellow strains against the wind on wooden stakes, and past them a slate-green sea chops under a sky bleached almost white. Held at chest height by an aunt, the whole frame leaning a touch to the left, heads nearly clipped at the top, a smudge of out-of-focus pink skin just intruding at the lower right edge. Flat overhead sunlight, a stop too bright, so the highlights flare and the pebbles go chalky; skin glows warm butter-yellow while sky and water drift towards cool aqua; shadows muddy with a faint green tint. The plastic lens keeps nothing truly crisp, softness growing towards the edges, the four corners sinking into dusky falloff, a thin rainbow fringe on bright edges, gritty consumer-film grain, low washed contrast. Unposed and mid-shout, imperfect and loved. The picture carries no writing of any kind: clean corners without printed numbers, plain clothing, unbranded cones and pails, nothing lettered on the windbreaks. Thanks.

name: a-glossy-optimism-picnic
prompt: Camera pressed into the turf at the foot of a smooth rolling hill, tilted upward, so tall blades of vivid emerald grass frame the bottom of the tall portrait picture, the closest ones razor sharp and beaded with dew, the farthest melting into soft green blur. Halfway up the slope a young family sprawls on a red-and-white checked rug beside a wicker basket: a mum, a dad and a little girl in crisp white and pale pastel clothes, all three mid-laugh with heads tipped back, while their golden retriever hangs in the air above them in a joyful leap, ears flapping, paws tucked. Big oily-sheened soap bubbles float everywhere, a couple of them huge and right against the lens, their skins swirling with pink, turquoise and gold. Over everything a deep, almost unreal cobalt sky, darker at the top, dotted with a few neat puffy white clouds, and a blazing noon sun peeking into one top corner, its star-shaped glare spilling a slanting trail of pale hexagonal flare rings down across the bubbles. The feel of a glossy mid-2000s advertising stock photo promising a bright tomorrow: wide-angle, high clean daylight, saturated and polished, slight glow blooming off the whites, firm contrast, not a speck of dirt, colours kept to sky blue, lawn green, bright white and sunny yellow. The picture carries no words, signs or printed marks of any kind. Thanks.

name: a-golden-hour-street-football
prompt: A single frame lifted from an old family tape, filmed one July evening around 2001 and dubbed to disc years later: soft and smeary, low in detail, colours bleeding a fraction past their edges, a fizz of grain in the darker areas. The setting is the turning circle at the end of a council-house close, rows of pebble-dashed semis with low brick walls and wheelie bins, the road surface still warm. A loose kickabout is under way, goals marked by two heaps of dumped sweatshirts, a mix of lanky teenagers and small kids in baggy shorts and plain knock-off football tops chasing a scuffed ball, while one boy of about twelve peels away after scoring, both arms stretched out like wings, shouting at the sky. Off to the side a woman in her fifties in a cardigan and slippers stands on her front step cradling a mug of tea, grinning at them. Seen from the far end of the street, zoomed all the way in so the houses compress into a flat stacked backdrop and the players overlap, the framing slightly tilted and handheld, as if a dad held it up from behind his garden gate. The sun sits low right behind the game: hair and shoulders outlined in glowing gold, a broad hazy flare smeared across the upper half, the sky blown to a milky cream that eats into the rooftops, and long skinny shadows running down the tarmac towards us. Shadows are grey and murky rather than black, reds slightly overcooked, the whole picture steeped in apricot, honey and washed-out rose. Candid, unposed, nobody aware of the lens: the feeling that the holidays have weeks left and it will never get dark. The image is clean of any writing, overlay, timecode or emblem; tops are blank and house numbers too blurry to read. Thanks.

name: b-school-photo-backdrop
prompt: A school picture-day portrait from around 2003, the kind of glossy print that came home in a cardboard folder with a sheet of wallet-sized copies. A figure in a plain black knitted balaclava sits upright on a low photographer's stool, shoulders turned slightly to one side the way pupils were always angled, chin a touch down, eyes looking dead into the lens with calm, polite stillness. Only the eyes show through the two eye holes; the knit is completely plain and unmarked. Black woollen gloves rest one over the other on its knee, and it wears a tidy navy V-neck school jumper over a white collared shirt, collar slightly crooked. Behind it hangs the familiar mottled canvas backdrop, cloudy grey-blue darkening toward the edges, softly out of focus. The light is flat and forgiving: a big soft main light from front-left and a gentle fill, so the mask and eyes are evenly lit with a small catchlight in each eye and almost no shadow, plus a faint hair light rimming the top of the head. Head-and-shoulders crop, centred, medium telephoto compression, camera at chest height. The colour is that slightly too-smooth, warm-skewed minilab print of the era: lifted blacks, creamy highlights, a gentle magenta-blue cast, fine grain and the soft sheen of photo paper. Ordinary, wholesome, and very wrong. The print is clean: no writing, digits, name plates or stamps.

name: b-camcorder-party-guest
prompt: A still lifted from somebody's family videotape, late 1990s, a birthday do in a cramped front room filmed by an uncle with a palm-sized tape camcorder. Twisted paper streamers in red, green and yellow droop from the light fitting, a balloon has drifted against the woodchip wallpaper, and a folding table under a plastic party cloth holds sausage rolls on a foil tray, a bowl of crisps, a hedgehog of cheese-and-pineapple sticks stuck in half a grapefruit, a wobbly orange jelly and paper cups. Behind the table the relatives are dancing to something on the stereo, cardigans and loud patterned shirts swinging, their arms and faces dragged into soft combed smears by the motion; a grandad in a paper crown is laughing at the back. Mid shot, the lens wide and slightly bowed at the frame edges. Closest to camera, filling the lower middle of the portrait frame, stands one extra guest in a plain dark-grey knitted ski mask and plain knitted gloves, the wool unpatterned and unmarked, nothing of them uncovered but a pair of eyes in the eye openings. One gloved hand holds a sagging paper plate with a single sausage roll on it. They have turned their head to meet the camcorder dead on, perfectly still, polite, patient, as though about to say thank you for having me. Nobody behind them has clocked it. The camcorder's built-in lamp blasts a flat, frontal, shadowless pool of white light onto the masked head and shoulders so the knit texture and both eye openings are crisp and evenly lit, while the room behind drops off into warm tungsten amber and muddy brown with a soft dark vignette. Tape-era texture: colours soft and smeared sideways past their edges, a red-orange glow bleeding off the foil and the bright cups, shadows noisy and crawling with grain, blacks milky and lifted, a slight handheld tilt. Warm, daft, happy and homely, with one guest who does not belong. The picture carries no words, digits, date overlay or symbols of any kind.

name: b-flash-digicam-funfair
prompt: A night photo from a travelling funfair around 2003, snapped on a cheap pocket digital camera with its built-in xenon flash going off at point-blank range, the sort of hasty holiday shot that later turns up in a happy throwback slideshow. Centre of the frame, seen from about the waist up and from slightly beneath, stands a figure in a plain dark-navy knitted ski mask and thick woollen gloves, body square to the lens, gazing straight out through the eye holes with mild, patient politeness; the knit is unpatterned and the whole face area is evenly lit, sharp and clear. In one gloved hand it holds a huge cloud of bubblegum-pink candyfloss on a paper stick; from the other hangs a tied clear plastic bag of water with a single orange goldfish won at a hook-a-duck stall. The flash makes the figure bright, flat and a little overexposed, with a hard dark shadow tucked close behind it, while everything further back falls away into night: the waltzer cars and the light-bulb arches of the rides are only long wobbly trails of magenta, lime, gold and electric blue where the slow shutter dragged them during a small hand shake, floating in a deep black sky speckled with coloured digital noise. Over-saturated early sensor colour, a cool blue tint on the flash-lit wool, purple fringing around the brightest lamps, mild softness at the edges, frame leaning a few degrees. Canopies and booths are plain blank fabric, and nothing in the image carries letters, numbers, signs or symbols. Thanks.

name: c-empty-summer-field-dusk
prompt: Vertical frame of a deserted recreation ground at the very end of a hot summer day, roughly 1999: knee-high meadow grass gone gold and feathery fills the bottom third, and half hidden in it lies a small kid's BMX dropped on its side, handlebars twisted, one pedal pointing at the sky. Behind it the field runs flat to a thin dark strip of oak trees and a single wooden bench, tiny and far away, and that low horizon sits well below the middle of the picture. The upper half is pure open sky, a smooth wash that starts as warm peach just above the trees and cools upward into a faded powder blue, empty of clouds, birds, wires and aircraft. The camera is a family handycam propped on a garden wall at adult eye level, left recording and untouched, framed straight and level, focus drifting slightly soft. The image has the gentle smeary quality of a tape transfer from a home video compilation: colours slightly bleached and rosy, the peach glowing and bleeding a touch into the tree line, a fine fizz of chroma speckle in the darkening grass, faint horizontal wobble near the bottom edge, highlights soft and milky. Mood: hushed, warm and a little heartbreaking, the moment after the last kid has been shouted home and the tape keeps rolling over nothing. The picture is clean of any writing, numbers, overlays or graphics.
